To hijack something means to forcefully take control of something that is already in motion or already underway, without permission, and redirect it toward your own purpose — against the will of whoever was rightfully in charge of it.

Three things are always happening at once when something is hijacked:

  1. Something was already moving or in progress, headed toward a specific goal.
  2. Someone seized control of it by force, threat, or aggressive pressure — without any right to do so.
  3. The original plan was interrupted and pulled in a completely different direction.

That combination — force + interception + redirection — is the soul of this word.

The clearest, most direct use of "hijack" is about vehicles. Picture this:

A plane takes off from New York, bound for London. Midway through the flight, a person threatens the pilots and says, "Don't fly to London. Fly to Cuba instead." The pilots comply because they have no choice. That person has just hijacked the plane.

The same thing can happen to a bus, a ship, or a truck. The person who does it is called a hijacker, and the act itself is called a hijacking. These are serious violent crimes. The hijacker's goal might be to make a political demand, rob the vehicle and its passengers, or escape somewhere without going through normal channels.

The key detail is that the vehicle was already in use, already on its way somewhere — the hijacker didn't steal an empty parked vehicle. They intercepted it mid-journey and took the wheel.
The Extended Meaning: Far Beyond Vehicles

This is where "hijack" becomes a truly powerful word to know, because modern English uses it constantly in non-vehicle situations. Wherever something is already underway and someone aggressively takes it over and steers it toward their own agenda, the word fits perfectly.

A conversation:
"She tried to talk about her problems, but her roommate hijacked the conversation and spent an hour talking about himself."
The conversation was already in motion. He took it over and redirected it — without her consent.

A meeting:
"The CEO had a clear agenda, but angry shareholders hijacked the meeting with demands he wasn't prepared for."
The meeting had a planned direction. It was forcefully pulled somewhere else.

A political or social movement:
"The peaceful protest was hijacked by a group of extremists who had a completely different agenda."
The movement stood for one thing; others took it over and redirected its energy for their own goals.

An idea or a plan:
"She came up with the entire concept, but her colleague hijacked it and presented it to the boss as his own."

An online hashtag:
"A company launched a feel-good hashtag campaign, but users hijacked it to publicly criticize the company's labor practices."
The company created the hashtag for one purpose; thousands of people seized it and steered it in the opposite direction.

In every single case, you'll find the same three elements: something already in motion → someone forcefully seizes control → it gets redirected away from its original purpose.

In computing and cybersecurity, "hijack" is used frequently and precisely:

Browser hijacking is when malicious software secretly takes control of your web browser — changing your homepage, redirecting your searches to different websites, or opening pages you never asked for. You didn't consent; something took over your browser and started steering it.

Session hijacking is when a hacker intercepts an active, ongoing connection between you and a website (say, your online bank account) and takes it over — pretending to be you.

DNS hijacking is when internet traffic you intended to send to one website gets secretly rerouted to a different one.

The pattern is the same: something already active and in use gets forcefully taken over and redirected without authorization.
The Weight and Feeling of the Word

"Hijack" is a strong, dramatic word. It is never neutral. When you use it, it always carries these feelings:

Aggression — The takeover wasn't gentle or polite. It was forced. Even when there's no physical weapon involved (as in a hijacked conversation), the word signals dominance, pressure, or manipulation.

Illegitimacy — The person taking control has no right to be in control. They are an intruder.

Violation — The rightful owner or operator loses control against their will. Something is being stolen from them — not a physical object, but direction, purpose, and authority.

This is why saying "he hijacked the conversation" is much stronger than saying "he changed the subject." You're signaling that it wasn't a polite shift — it was a hostile, unwanted takeover.

Hijack vs. Steal:
You steal a parked car from a parking lot. You hijack a moving bus. Stealing is about taking possession of something idle. Hijacking is about intercepting something that is actively in use and in motion.

Hijack vs. Take over:
"Take over" is neutral and can be perfectly legal — a company can take over another company through a proper business deal. "Hijack" always implies it is unauthorized, forced, and wrong.

Hijack vs. Commandeer:
To commandeer is to officially seize something by authority — like a military officer commandeering a civilian vehicle in wartime. It sounds formal and sanctioned. To hijack is always unauthorized and criminal or at least inappropriate.

Hijack vs. Derail:
To derail something means to disrupt and ruin it — knock it off course so it goes nowhere. To hijack something means to disrupt it AND then steer it toward your own destination. Derailing destroys the journey. Hijacking steals the journey.

To hijack something means:

→ To forcefully take control of something already in motion or in progress
→ Without permission, against the will of whoever is rightfully in charge
→ And redirect it for your own purpose

It works in the literal sense (seizing planes, buses, ships mid-journey), in everyday social situations (conversations, meetings, movements, ideas), and in the digital world (browsers, internet sessions, online trends).

Whenever you see or hear "hijack," picture someone grabbing the steering wheel of a moving vehicle from the driver's hands — that image captures the force, the wrongness, and the redirection that the word always carries, no matter what context it appears in.
